reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: The most common fibrous tumour of infancy, frequently present at birth or arising in the first two years of life
Presents as solitary or multiple firm nodules involving skin, subcutis, muscle, bone and, less commonly, viscera
Solitary and multicentric forms without visceral involvement generally carry an excellent prognosis
Germline or somatic PDGFRB mutations underlie many familial and sporadic cases, with some cases involving NOTCH3
Histology shows a biphasic pattern of plump myofibroblastic nodules with a more cellular, primitive haemangiopericytoma-like zone
A characteristic zonation with peripheral mature myoid nodules and a central immature cellular component is typical
Many lesions, especially solitary ones, regress spontaneously, so observation is often appropriate
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile myofibromatosis is a benign proliferation of myofibroblasts arising as solitary, multicentric or generalised disease. A substantial proportion is driven by activating mutations in PDGFRB, a receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes myofibroblastic proliferation, and the gene can be involved in both familial and sporadic forms. Lesions typically display a distinctive biphasic architecture, with nodules of mature spindled myoid cells at the periphery surrounding a more cellular, primitive zone containing thin-walled branching vessels. Spontaneous regression is common and is thought to reflect apoptosis and involution of the proliferating cells.
additionalInvestigations: MRI or ultrasound to map solitary versus multicentric disease and assess deep structures
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude visceral involvement in generalised forms
Biopsy with histological assessment of the biphasic myofibroblastic pattern
Molecular testing for PDGFRB or NOTCH3 alterations in appropriate cases
Immunohistochemistry showing smooth-muscle actin positivity with myofibroblastic differentiation
redFlags: Visceral or multiorgan (generalised) involvement in a neonate, which carries higher morbidity
Respiratory or gastrointestinal compromise from visceral lesions
Rapid growth or atypical histology raising concern for infantile fibrosarcoma
Lesions causing organ dysfunction or airway obstruction
reference.prognosis: Solitary and multicentric disease without visceral involvement has an excellent outlook, with frequent spontaneous regression. Generalised disease with visceral involvement carries a higher risk of morbidity and mortality, particularly in the neonatal period, though many still improve with supportive care.
pitfalls: Confusing the cellular immature zone with infantile fibrosarcoma
Overtreating a solitary lesion likely to regress spontaneously
Failing to assess for visceral disease in an infant with multiple lesions
Assuming all forms share the same benign course regardless of visceral involvement
